3. After investigation the Investigating Officer submitted charge-sheet against 4 persons namely-Amir Hossain, Md. Hossain, Jesmin Akter and Mofazzal Hossain Khan @ Mofa under section 302/114/34 of the Penal Code, 1860. The case record was transmitted to the Court of learned Sessions Judge, Laxmipur for trial and that was registered as Sessions Case No. 64 of 2006. Ultimately, the case was transferred to the Court of learned Additional Sessions Judge, Laxmipur for trial and the learned Additional Sessions Judge framed charges against the accused persons under section 302/114/34 of the Penal Code, 1860. The charges were read over to the accused persons to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 

 7. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, Laxmipur on completion of the trial passed the judgment and order dated 13-5-2008 where only the condemned prisoner was found guilty under section 302 of the Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced him to death by hanging and also awarded a fine of Taka 25,000 and acquitted other accused persons. 

 10. Mr. Syed Mahbubur Rahman, the learned advocate-on-record, appearing for the appellant, has taken us through the F.I.R. the inquest report, the postmortem report, the charge-sheet, the testimonies of the witnesses, the judgment and order passed by the trial court and the High Court Division, the connected materials on record and submits that the High Court Division erred both in law and fact in passing the aforesaid judgment accepting the death reference and dismissing the appeals. He further submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the examination of the accused under section 342 of the Code of. Criminal Procedure by the trial Court is highly defective because any incriminating piece of evidence of the prosecution witnesses in any way was not brought to the notice of the appellant. So the appellant remained totally in dark about the evidence adduced against him, so he could not take his defence properly for which he has been highly prejudiced. He also submits that the moot point of the case ought to have been decided that whether the condemned prisoner was insane at the time of alleged commission of the offence. There is sufficient evidence in the case from the prosecution such as P.Ws. 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 14 who admitted categorically that the accused was insane/mad at the time of commission of the offence. So High Court Division ought to have considered whether or not the prosecution witnesses support this point vehemently. The condemned prisoner ought to have been acquitted in the case as section 84 of the Penal Code, 1860 provides that "nothing is an-offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law" and for non-consideration of this important point the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. 

 33. P.W. 19, Md. Abdul Awal Chowdhury, the Investigating Officer, in his examination-in-chief stated that on 20-05-2006 he was posted as SI at Ramgonj Police Station and in pursuance of order of the Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station he investigated the instant case. He stated that he went to the place of occurrence and prepared sketch map with index. He proved the sketch map and index and his signature on it, which was marked as Exhibits 4, 4/1 and 5, 5/1 and 5(ka), 5(ka)/1. He stated that after arriving to the place of occurrence, he held inquest on the corpse of the deceased and prepared the inquest report and sent the dead body to morgue. He also stated that he seized alamots and prepared seizure-list. He stated that he recorded the statements of the witnesses under section 161 of the Code. He stated that after completion of investigation, he submitted charge-sheet being No. 21 dated 5-7-2006 under section 302/114/34 of the Penal Code, 1860. During cross-examination, he stated that he arrested the accused Mofazzal Hossen from the place of occurrence and that he was not found as a person of unsound mind. He denied the defence suggestion that the accused was mad at the time of occurrence. He denied the defence suggestion that he conducted the investigation being influenced and submitted the charge-sheet. 

 1. The defence claimed that the appellant was a person of unsound mind at the time of occurrence and he is entitled to get the benefit of General Exception as provided under section 84 of the Penal Code, 1860. 

 39. Sections 76-106 of the Penal Code, 1860 deal with the provisions of General Exception. If any offence is committed, but falls within any of the General Exceptions enumerated in sections 76-106, then the offence has been made exempted from punishment. The defence has taken the plea of section 84 of the Penal Code i.e. when the offence was committed, the appellant was a person of unsound mind. section 84 of the Penal Code runs as follows: 

 44. It was held in the case of Md. Abdul Majid Sarkar vs. State [40 DLR (AD) 83] that," section 105 of the Evidence Act, 1872 casts a burden upon the accused to prove the existence of circumstances bringing the case within any special exception or proviso contained in other part of the same (Penal) Code, 1860". The same view was also reiterated by this Division in the case of Shah Alam vs. State [42 DLR (AD) 31] with observation that, "In a criminal case the accused are not required to set up their case in writing, such as a written statement of the defendant of a civil suit, nor are they required to give evidence to prove their innocence, or even to establish their pleas, except a special plea within the meaning of section 105, Evidence Act........."
